goldens.comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 3 | `app/models/topic_embed.rb:48` | Host validation covers only the initial URL; redirects or DNS rebinding can pivot `open(url)` to internal services or cloud metadata. | security | 75

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb:48, the code uses `open(url).read` from the 'open-uri' library to fetch remote content. The URL validation at line 11 only checks if the URL starts with 'http://' or 'https://' using a regex. There's no validation that the URL's host matches an allowed/safe host. The `open` method from open-uri will follow HTTP redirects automatically, meaning an attacker could provide a URL that redirects to internal services (like http://169.254.169.254 for cloud metadata, or internal network resources). This is a classic SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) vulnerability. The finding correctly identifies that while there may be some host validation elsewhere (embeddable_host setting), the import_remote method itself doesn't validate the host before making the request, and redirects can bypass any initial URL validation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 4 | `app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:15` | Every cache miss enqueues before throttling occurs, permitting repeated iframe loads to grow the Sidekiq backlog. | performance | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the embed_controller.rb code at line 15, when topic_id is nil, it enqueues a job with `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)`. The throttling logic is in TopicRetriever.retrieved_recently? which uses Redis setnx with 60 second expiry. However, the job is enqueued BEFORE any throttling check happens - the throttling only occurs inside the job execution in TopicRetriever.retrieve(). This means every cache miss (when TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed returns nil) will add a job to the Sidekiq queue, regardless of throttling. Multiple iframe loads for the same embed_url will each enqueue a separate job. While the jobs themselves will be throttled during execution (only one will actually perform_retrieve), the queue can still grow with redundant jobs. This is a real performance concern - the finding correctly identifies that jobs are enqueued before throttling occurs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 5 | `lib/topic_retriever.rb:41` | Every distinct missing URL can trigger a complete feed poll, multiplying remote downloads, parsing, and database work. | performance | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb:41, the code in perform_retrieve() checks if feed_polling_enabled? and if so calls Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({}). This happens for every unique embed_url that hasn't been retrieved recently (60 second throttle per URL). The poll_feed job downloads and parses the entire RSS feed and processes all items. So if 10 different URLs are requested within a short time, the feed could be polled 10 times. However, there's a 60-second per-URL throttle in retrieved_recently?, and the feed polling itself has some protection (it checks if TopicEmbed exists before and after). The finding is partially valid - multiple distinct URLs can trigger multiple feed polls, but the impact is somewhat mitigated. This is a real architectural concern where each new URL triggers a full feed poll.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 6 | `app/models/topic_embed.rb:48` | Remote article bodies are read completely without a size bound, risking worker memory exhaustion. | performance | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb:48, the code is `doc = Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)`. This uses `open(url).read` which reads the entire remote content into memory without any size limit. A malicious or misconfigured remote URL could serve an extremely large response, causing memory exhaustion on the worker. This is a real performance/security concern - there's no Content-Length check, no streaming, and no size limit on the read operation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 7 | `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:35` | A malformed item aborts the complete feed loop; retries and per-item error isolation are both absent, potentially blocking later entries indefinitely. | reliability | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb lines 30-36, the poll_feed method iterates over rss.items with `rss.items.each do |i|`. Inside the loop, it accesses `i.link`, `i.id`, `i.content`, and `i.title`. If any of these operations fail (e.g., content is nil and .scrub fails, or other malformed data), an exception would be raised and the entire loop would abort, preventing processing of subsequent items. There's no begin/rescue block around the individual item processing. This is a real reliability issue - a single malformed RSS item could prevent all subsequent items from being processed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 8 | `app/models/topic_embed.rb:37` | `content_sha1` advances even if `PostRevisor#revise!` fails, permanently marking stale content as current. | reliability | 75

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 30-38, the update logic is: 1) Call revisor.revise!() to update the post, 2) Then call embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1). The issue is that revise! can fail (return false), but the code doesn't check the return value before updating content_sha1. If revise! fails, the content_sha1 will still be updated to the new value, meaning future attempts to update will think the content is already current (since content_sha1 matches) even though the actual post content was never updated. This is a real reliability bug - the code should check if revise! succeeded before updating the hash.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 9 | `spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:43` | The test expects synchronous `TopicRetriever#retrieve`, but the controller now enqueues a job, making the spec deterministically fail and leaving the enqueue contract unverified. | testing | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the test in spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb lines 40-47, the test sets up expectations: TopicEmbed.expects(:topic_id_for_embed).returns(nil), then creates a mock retriever and expects TopicRetriever.new to return it, and retriever.expects(:retrieve). However, looking at the controller code in embed_controller.rb lines 12-15, when topic_id is nil, it calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...) which is an async job, not TopicRetriever.new directly. The TopicRetriever is actually called inside the job (lib/jobs/regular/retrieve_topic.rb). So the test is expecting synchronous TopicRetriever instantiation but the controller enqueues a job instead. This means the test's expectations (TopicRetriever.expects(:new).returns(retriever)) will never be satisfied because TopicRetriever.new is not called directly in the controller - it's called in the background job. This is a real test/implementation mismatch.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 10 | `db/migrate/20131219203905_add_cook_method_to_posts.rb:3` | Default `cook_method: 1` means `raw_html`, so all existing and ordinary new posts bypass the normal cooking pipeline. | data-migration | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in Post model (app/models/post.rb), the cook_methods enum is defined as: `@cook_methods ||= Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)`. In Ruby Enum, the first value (:regular) gets index 0, and :raw_html gets index 1. The migration sets default to 1, which corresponds to :raw_html. However, examining the cook method in Post: `return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` - this means posts with cook_method=1 (raw_html) would bypass cooking. But wait - looking at PostCreator in lib/post_creator.rb, it only sets cook_method when explicitly passed: `post.cook_method = @opts[:cook_method] if @opts[:cook_method].present?`. So new posts without explicit cook_method would get the database default of 1 (raw_html), which would indeed bypass the cooking pipeline. This is a real bug - the default should be 0 (regular) not 1 (raw_html).

adjudication_records.issue_text: 11 | `db/migrate/20131219203905_add_cook_method_to_posts.rb:3` | Adding a non-null defaulted column directly to a large posts table may rewrite and lock it, causing deployment downtime. | data-migration | 75

adjudication.rationale: The migration adds a column with a default value and NOT NULL constraint to the posts table: `add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false`. In older versions of PostgreSQL (before 11), this operation would rewrite the entire table and hold an exclusive lock, which could cause significant downtime for large tables. The posts table is typically one of the largest tables in a Discourse installation. This is a legitimate concern for production deployments, though the severity depends on the database version and table size.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 13 | `app/models/topic_embed.rb:22` | Feed content is stored as decoded, unsanitized `raw_html`, permitting executable elements, event attributes, and dangerous URL schemes. | adversarial | 100

adjudication.rationale: The finding is accurate. In app/models/topic_embed.rb, the import method takes `contents` and passes it to PostCreator with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. Looking at app/models/post.rb lines 131-133, when cook_method is raw_html, the cook method returns `raw` directly without any sanitization. The contents come from RSS feeds (poll_feed.rb uses CGI.unescapeHTML on content) or from ruby-readability parsing. While readability does filter some tags, the raw_html cook method bypasses Discourse's normal post cooking/sanitization pipeline. The test in topic_embed_spec.rb confirms this: `post.cooked.should == post.raw`. This means any HTML in the imported content, including script tags, event handlers, or dangerous URL schemes, would be rendered directly without sanitization, creating an XSS vulnerability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 14 | `app/models/topic_embed.rb:48` | Redirect destinations, resolved addresses, and ports are unconstrained after initial validation, enabling redirect-based SSRF and arbitrary-port access. | adversarial | 75

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb:48, the code uses `open(url).read` via ruby-readability to fetch remote content. The URL validation at line 11 only checks if the URL starts with 'http://' or 'https://' using a regex. The `open()` function (from open-uri) will follow HTTP redirects automatically, and there's no validation of where those redirects lead. An attacker could provide a URL that redirects to internal services (127.0.0.1, internal hostnames, cloud metadata endpoints like 169.254.169.254, etc.) or to arbitrary ports. This is a legitimate Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability. The initial URL validation is insufficient because it doesn't constrain the final destination after redirects.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 15 | `lib/topic_retriever.rb:26` | URL-specific throttling is bypassed with unique paths or queries; each miss can amplify into queue, Redis, HTTP, feed, CPU, and database work. | adversarial | 100

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the throttling mechanism in topic_retriever.rb uses the full embed_url as the key for Redis throttling. This means an attacker could bypass the 60-second throttle by using different query parameters or paths (e.g., http://example.com/page?v=1, http://example.com/page?v=2, etc.). Each unique URL would be treated as a separate key, allowing unlimited requests that trigger HTTP fetches, RSS polling, database operations, and other expensive work. The code at line 26 shows `retrieved_key = "retrieved:#{@embed_url}"` which confirms this per-URL throttling approach. This is a real denial-of-service vulnerability where an adversary can amplify resource consumption by varying URL parameters.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 16 | `app/models/topic_embed.rb:64` | URL rewriting mishandles protocol-relative references and leaves document-relative references unresolved, breaking imported links and images. | correctness | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the absolutize_urls method in topic_embed.rb (lines 54-73), it only handles URLs that start with '/'. The code checks `if href.present? && href.start_with?('/')` for links and `if src.present? && src.start_with?('/')` for images. This means: 1) Protocol-relative URLs (starting with '//') would be incorrectly prefixed with the full URL since they start with '/', resulting in malformed URLs like 'http://example.com//cdn.example.com/image.jpg'. 2) Document-relative URLs (like 'images/foo.jpg' without leading slash) are completely ignored and left as-is, which would break when the content is displayed on a different domain. This is a real correctness bug in URL handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 17 | `lib/topic_retriever.rb:15` | Case-sensitive, unnormalized hostname comparison rejects equivalent DNS hostnames and leaves the iframe loading indefinitely. | correctness | 75

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb:15, the code does `SiteSetting.embeddable_host != URI(@embed_url).host`. This comparison is case-sensitive in Ruby (string comparison). DNS hostnames are case-insensitive per RFC, so 'EvilTrout.com' and 'eviltrout.com' should be equivalent but would fail this check. Additionally, there's no normalization for trailing dots or other DNS equivalences. If a user visits from a URL with different casing than what's configured in embeddable_host, the check would fail and the topic wouldn't be retrieved. This is a real correctness issue - the hostname comparison should use case-insensitive comparison (e.g., using downcase on both sides).

adjudication_records.issue_text: 18 | `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:29` | The complete feed and every item are processed without size or item-count limits, allowing a feed to monopolize a worker. | performance | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the poll_feed.rb code, the execute method calls poll_feed which uses SimpleRSS.parse on the feed URL and then iterates through rss.items with rss.items.each. There are no limits on the number of items processed or the size of the feed content. A malicious or very large feed could indeed cause the worker to process an unbounded number of items. However, this is a scheduled job that runs hourly (recurrence { hourly }), and RSS feeds typically have reasonable item counts. The finding is technically valid - there's no explicit limit on items processed - but the practical impact is limited since: 1) it's a scheduled background job, 2) RSS feeds are typically bounded in practice, 3) the admin controls the feed URL. This is a real but low-severity performance concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 19 | `lib/topic_retriever.rb:27` | The throttle is claimed before retrieval succeeds and is not cleared on failure, causing retries inside 60 seconds to silently skip the fetch. | reliability | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in lib/topic_retriever.rb, the `retrieved_recently?` method sets a Redis key with `setnx` and a 60-second expiry BEFORE `perform_retrieve` is called. If `perform_retrieve` fails (e.g., network error, parsing error, etc.), the throttle key remains set, and any retry within 60 seconds will return early from `retrieved_recently?` returning true. This means failed retrieval attempts block retries for 60 seconds. The finding correctly identifies that the throttle is set before success is confirmed and is not cleared on failure, which could cause silent skipping of fetch retries. This is a real reliability issue in the code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 20 | `app/models/topic_embed.rb:48` | Article retrieval lacks explicit connection/read deadlines and response-size controls, allowing slow origins to exhaust workers. | reliability | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb:48, the code uses `open(url).read` from the open-uri library to fetch remote content. This is called in `import_remote` method. The code indeed lacks explicit timeout settings and response size limits. When using open-uri's `open()` without timeout options, it uses Ruby's default socket timeouts which can be very long or indefinite. A malicious or slow origin server could cause workers to hang indefinitely. Additionally, there's no limit on response size, so a large response could consume excessive memory. This is a real reliability/security concern - the code should use explicit timeouts like `open(url, read_timeout: 30, open_timeout: 10)` and potentially limit response size.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 21 | `lib/topic_retriever.rb:50` | A missing importer user silently terminates retrieval, leaving an endlessly reloading iframe without an actionable failure signal. | reliability | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb lines 48-53, the fetch_http method does indeed silently return if the user is blank: `return if user.blank?`. This is called from perform_retrieve, and if the user doesn't exist, the retrieval silently fails. Meanwhile, in app/views/embed/loading.html.erb, there's a 30-second auto-reload: `setTimeout(function() { document.location.reload(); }, 30000);`. If embed_by_username is misconfigured or the user doesn't exist, the iframe will keep reloading indefinitely with no error message. This is a real reliability issue - the code silently fails without any feedback to the user or admin about the misconfiguration.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 22 | `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:29` | Feed retrieval has no explicit network deadlines and retries are disabled, delaying recovery until a later hourly run. | reliability | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb line 29, the code uses `open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` from the 'open-uri' library without any timeout configuration. The finding correctly identifies that there's no explicit network deadline - if the feed server is slow or unresponsive, the request could hang indefinitely. Additionally, `sidekiq_options retry: false` is set on line 12, meaning if the job fails due to a timeout or network issue, it won't retry until the next hourly scheduled run. This is a real reliability concern - network operations without timeouts can cause worker threads to hang, and disabling retries means transient failures won't be recovered from quickly.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 23 | `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:35` | Poller tests mock the parsing path and miss that valid RSS items with `description` but no `content` abort the import. | testing | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the poll_feed.rb code at line 35, it accesses `i.content` on RSS items. The finding claims that RSS items with `description` but no `content` would cause issues. However, examining the code: `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` - if `i.content` is nil, calling `.scrub` on nil would raise a NoMethodError. This is a valid concern. The tests in poll_feed_spec.rb only test the execute method's conditional logic (checking settings) and mock `poll_feed`, never actually testing the RSS parsing logic with real or mock RSS data. adjudication_records.issue_text: 24 | `app/models/topic_embed.rb:11` | URL tests miss hostless values such as `http://`, which pass the prefix regex and can create invalid embed mappings. | testing | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb line 11, the regex check is `return unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//`. This regex checks if the URL starts with 'http://' or 'https://'. The finding claims that 'http://' alone (without a host) would pass this check. This is technically true - a string like 'http://' would match the regex `^https?\:\/\/` because it only checks for the protocol prefix, not for a valid host after it. However, looking at the actual usage in the codebase, URLs come from RSS feeds (i.link or i.id) or from embed_url parameters. While the regex is indeed permissive, the practical impact is limited since malformed URLs would likely fail later when used (e.g., in URI parsing at line 52-53 or when making HTTP requests). The finding identifies a real gap in input validation - the regex doesn't validate that there's actually a host component after the protocol.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 25 | `app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:9` | Invalid or cross-host `embed_url` values receive a successful loading page and are repeatedly enqueued instead of returning an actionable client error. | api-contract | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the embed_controller.rb, the `best` action calls `TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed(embed_url)` and if no topic_id is found, it enqueues a job and renders 'loading'. The `ensure_embeddable` before_filter validates the referer host matches `embeddable_host`, but does NOT validate the `embed_url` parameter itself. In `topic_retriever.rb`, the `invalid_host?` method checks if `SiteSetting.embeddable_host != URI(@embed_url).host`, which would prevent retrieval for cross-host URLs. However, the job is still enqueued in the controller before this check happens in the job. The loading page with auto-refresh is returned regardless of whether the embed_url is valid. This means: 1) A user can submit any embed_url and get a loading page that refreshes every 30 seconds, 2) Jobs are enqueued even for invalid URLs (though they won't process), 3) No error feedback is given to the client. This is a real issue - invalid embed_urls should return an error rather than a loading page that keeps refreshing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 26 | `app/models/topic_embed.rb:78` | Exact raw-string URL identity lacks canonicalization, so equivalent URLs can fragment comments across duplicate topics. | api-contract | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed does a simple WHERE query on embed_url. The finding claims that equivalent URLs (like with/without trailing slash, different query param order, etc.) could create duplicate topics. This is a valid concern - the code at line 78 does `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: embed_url).pluck(:topic_id).first` which is an exact string match. However, this is more of a design consideration than a bug - the code works as designed (exact URL matching). The import method also uses exact matching. While URL canonicalization could be beneficial, the current implementation is consistent and functional. This is more of a feature request/enhancement than a bug or defect. The code correctly stores and retrieves URLs as provided - it's not broken, just potentially could be more robust.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 27 | `app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:26` | The endpoint requires an optional `Referer` header, breaking legitimate embeds that suppress it through privacy controls or `Referrer-Policy`. | api-contract | 75

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in app/controllers/embed_controller.rb line 26, the ensure_embeddable method checks `URI(request.referer || '').host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. If request.referer is nil or empty (which happens when browsers suppress the Referer header due to privacy settings, Referrer-Policy, or cross-origin restrictions), then URI('').host returns nil, which would not equal the embeddable_host, causing the request to be rejected with 'invalid referer host'. This is a real functional issue - legitimate embed requests from pages that don't send Referer headers will fail. The spec in embed_controller_spec.rb confirms this behavior: 'it raises an error with no referer' shows this is intentional but problematic for real-world usage where Referer headers are often suppressed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 28 | `db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:3` | `force: true` drops an existing `topic_embeds` table, turning migration-state mismatches into silent data loss. | data-migration | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb, I can see `create_table :topic_embeds, force: true`. The `force: true` option in Rails migrations will drop an existing table before creating a new one. This is indeed problematic in a migration context because: 1) Migrations should be idempotent and safe to run, 2) If the table already exists with data (perhaps from a failed partial migration or manual creation), using `force: true` would silently destroy that data, 3) The standard practice is to use `create_table` without `force: true` so that if the table exists, the migration fails explicitly rather than destroying data. This is a real data safety concern in production migration scenarios.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 29 | `db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3` | Adding `force: true` to the existing migration can drop populated `top_topics` data during replay or inconsistent migration bookkeeping. | data-migration | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb, the change is adding `force: true` to `create_table :top_topics`. The `force: true` option in Rails migrations causes the table to be dropped if it already exists before creating it. This is a real problem because if this migration is replayed (e.g., during a database reset or if migration bookkeeping gets inconsistent), it would drop any existing data in the top_topics table. This is a legitimate data safety concern for production environments where the table might already contain data.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 30 | `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:35` | A nil-content poison item aborts all later imports on every poll because the job disables retries and lacks item isolation. | adversarial | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the poll_feed.rb code at line 35, the code iterates through rss.items and calls `i.content.scrub` on each item. If `i.content` is nil, calling `.scrub` on nil would raise a NoMethodError, which would abort the entire job since `sidekiq_options retry: false` is set. However, the finding claims this is about 'nil-content poison item' - let me verify: `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` - if i.content is nil, then nil.scrub would fail. This is a real bug because: 1) RSS feeds can have items without content, 2) The job has retry disabled, 3) There's no error handling around individual items, so one bad item would prevent all subsequent items from being processed. This is a legitimate correctness issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 31 | `app/models/topic_embed.rb:36` | The update path advances its verification hash after a rejected or non-raising failed revision, creating a silent-pass state that never retries stale content. | adversarial | 75

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb around line 36, the update path calls `revisor.revise!` and then unconditionally calls `embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1)` on line 36. The `revise!` method returns a boolean indicating success/failure, but this return value is not checked. If the revision fails (returns false), the content_sha1 is still updated, which would prevent future retry attempts since the hash would match even though the content wasn't actually updated. This is a real bug - the code should only update the content_sha1 if the revision succeeded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: 32 | `app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:26` | Case-sensitive hostname comparison makes the public boundary depend on textual DNS casing; the same behavior is duplicated in `TopicRetriever`. | api-contract | 100

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in app/controllers/embed_controller.rb line 26, the code does `URI(request.referer || '').host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. Similarly in lib/topic_retriever.rb line 14, it does `SiteSetting.embeddable_host != URI(@embed_url).host`. The URI.host method returns the hostname as-is from the URL, and the comparison is done with `!=` which is case-sensitive in Ruby for strings. DNS hostnames are case-insensitive per RFC, so 'EvilTrout.com' and 'eviltrout.com' should be treated as the same host, but this code would treat them as different. This is a real security/correctness issue - an attacker could potentially bypass the embeddable_host check by using different casing in the URL, or legitimate users with differently-cased URLs would be incorrectly rejected.
